Harbour town votes to keep its ferry, and to pay for it

Alice Moreau · Fri 18 Sep 2026 06.00

The ferry has crossed the estuary eleven times a day since 1931, and for most of that time nobody in the town gave it a second thought, until the operator announced in March that the winter timetable would be its last.

On Thursday night, after a meeting that ran past midnight, residents voted by a wide margin to take the service over themselves and to raise the harbour levy to pay for it.

We are not sentimental about a boat. We are practical about a bridge that is forty minutes away by road, and an ambulance that has to drive it.

That was the argument that carried the room, according to several people who were there, and it was made by a councillor who had opposed the plan until a week ago.

The levy will rise by about the price of two return tickets a year for a typical household, which the campaign had printed on every leaflet it delivered.

“About the price of two return tickets a year”

Not everybody was persuaded. Owners of the holiday lets along the front, who pay the levy but rarely use the boat, asked for an exemption and were refused.

Their representative said afterwards that they would not challenge the result, but that they expected the accounts to be published every quarter, in full.

The handover is planned for the first of January. Until then the present operator will run the winter timetable as announced, with one boat instead of two.

A public meeting to elect the board of the new company will be held in the lifeboat station next month, and nominations are already open.
